# Professional Services

`customer_support.offering.service.professional_services` · offering_type · parent `customer_support.offering.service`

> Bounded, scoped work delivered against a statement of work — implementation, migration, integration, training — usually attached to a product the same company sells. The defining structural fact is the deadline: professional services work has a go-live, and the go-live is frequently the client's, not ours. That converts every support contact inside the delivery window into a schedule risk, and it means urgency here is set by a date on someone else's calendar rather than by the severity of the fault. The second fact is that this type sits directly on the product/service seam and is where the hybrid family's sorting problem actually lands. A client hitting a defect during implementation is hitting OUR product, but they are hitting it inside work WE scoped, so the question "is this a bug or is this scope?" arrives with a commercial answer attached and a deadline pressing on it. Support is usually the first function to see the answer and the last to be allowed to give it. The third is that the engagement ends. Unlike managed services, there is a handover, and the handover is where support inherits an account it did not build, configured in ways nobody documented, with expectations set by people who have moved to the next project. Most post-implementation support pain is a documentation failure committed months earlier by a team that was measured on delivery date. The habit carried in from managed services and punished here is assuming continuity. There is no standing relationship after go-live unless someone deliberately built one.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| delivery | scoped work against a statement of work, with a defined start, a defined end and a go-live |
| pricing_shape | fixed fee against milestones, or time and materials with a cap — priced per engagement, and change requests priced separately |
| margin_profile | set at scoping and largely fixed thereafter; unbilled support inside the delivery window is the main way a profitable engagement becomes an unprofitable one |
| post_sale_load | concentrated and time-boxed — heavy through delivery, spiking at go-live, then dropping to near zero at handover unless a support contract picks it up |
| support_load | deadline-shaped rather than volume-shaped. Contact rate tracks proximity to go-live far more than it tracks the number of users, and the same defect reported eight weeks out and two days out are different-severity events |
| resolution_locus | genuinely split — our product, the client's environment, the configuration we built, or the scope we agreed. Naming which one is a commercial act as much as a technical one |
| notes | The scope conversation is the one that actually decides margin, and it is decided in the first reply to the ticket rather than in a later negotiation. An agent who answers "yes we can do that" has priced a change request without knowing it.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `expires_at`


> Entitlement here is the statement of work and it EXPIRES at handover — usually with no event, no notification and no change in how the client behaves. Continuing to serve an expired professional-services engagement is the single most common source of silent unbilled work in this family, and the expiry date is the only thing that catches it.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.commitment`

Requires `promised_at`, `due_at`, `owner_ref`


> Commitments made during delivery are schedule dependencies in the client's plan, not courtesies. Missing one moves their go-live, which is why this type treats an unmet commitment as more serious than a missed SLA — the SLA affects our reporting and the commitment affects their launch.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `customer_account_ref`, `resolution_type`


> resolution_type is where the bug-or-scope answer is recorded. Without it the engagement cannot report how much of its support load was product defect versus scope creep, which is precisely the number needed to scope the next engagement correctly.

## Metadata

owner **Customer Support** · updated 2026-08-08 · review **unreviewed** · confidence **provisional**


> This type inherits the family's deflection deactivations and should. The arguable case is training and enablement content, which genuinely does recur across engagements — but it is authored by delivery for the client's users rather than by support for its own queue, so it is not the same programme wearing a different name. If a firm runs implementations at volume against a single product, revisit this: at that point the type is behaving like managed_services and the reactivation there is the better model.
